context:COMP.summary: Today OpenHeart only really handles Java, from source and at the syntax level. Kotlin is parsed with the Java grammar, other languages fall back to the JavaScript grammar, and the JDK is 12 stubs. Points-to, IFDS and taint are placeholders, queries are a few fixed internal Rust functions, and 'incremental' is a hash XOR. XMI emits class names only. There is no SARIF, GraphML, LSP or usable CI artefact. Against Joern, CodeQL, SootUp, WALA, OPAL, Doop, Semgrep, Infer and PhASAR the gap is large on every analysis dimension. Against IntelliJ, Visual Paradigm (VP), Enterprise Architect (EA) and Sourcetrail it leads only on diagram breadth. Fix frontends, analyses and benchmarks first.

context:AUTO.summary: I ran all 12 checks without cargo. The syntax gates all pass: 21/21 JS files plus the inline index.html module, 8/8 Python files, 23/23 JSON files, 3/3 workflow YAMLs and 3/3 shell scripts. All 198 .rs files are reachable from lib.rs or main.rs, and the scan found no secrets in the working tree or in 154 commits. The serious problems came from reading the code behind the checks. /api/source lets any client read any file on the server: the server listens on 0.0.0.0 and sends CORS *. repo_url is passed to git clone without validation. Four unsafe blocks in the ROBDD module can use freed memory. Twelve of the committed showcase diagrams carry hash values that never appear in the code. Kotlin, TypeScript and Rust are parsed with the Java or JavaScript grammar. The F1 metric scores 1.0 on empty sets. The Docker image cannot build or start. Code duplication is 35% in the diagram exporters and 13% across src/, and 29.6% of public items have rustdoc comments. Scripts are in C:\Users\AHMAD_~1\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\D--Repos-OpenHeart\31873741-1e3a-46df-bb5d-a94a867cbe24\scratchpad\audit-auto

context:BENCH.summary: OpenHeart has no benchmark-grade evaluation yet. Its headline accuracy figure (F1 = 1.0000 across six languages) compares simple class-name sets. One side comes from a keyword regex, the other from the engine's own keyword heuristic, and both are filtered by a shared denylist: 184 of the engine's 188 excluded names also appear in the oracle's list. The repositories it was measured on are unpinned and gitignored. The space and latency claims (128x, 4.65 MB per 1M nodes, about 1 ns lookups, zero-copy loading) have no benchmark code. The structures in the code contradict them: about 25 B per node on disk and about 210 B per node in RAM. What the docs call 'IFDS' and 'Andersen' analyses are local marking passes. OpenHeart Bench below proposes 15 suites, one per output, each with external oracles, pinned corpora, re-run competitor baselines and CI gates.

lens:WSEC.summary: The web studio is a ~9K-line vanilla-JS single-page app deployed statically to GitHub Pages with no backend in the default deployment, so there is no GitHub token to leak (all API calls are anonymous) and no server-side attack surface on Pages — genuinely good from a secrets standpoint. The SVG card renderer (uml-card-renderer.js) is disciplined: every interpolated value goes through escapeXml and is emitted as an inert data: URI, and the file tree, breadcrumbs and code viewer use textContent or escapeHtml-before-highlight, so imported source code cannot inject tags there. However, the central weakness is a pervasive "build an HTML string and assign innerHTML" pattern in the inline bootstrap module of index.html, with no Content-Security-Policy, no Trusted Types, and no Subresource Integrity on five third-party CDN scripts. The result is a reachable DOM-based XSS: attacker-controlled file paths from a public GitHub repo tree (or entry paths inside a loaded ZIP) and repo/codebase names flow unescaped into hudText.innerHTML progress messages and into the localStorage-backed project-history dropdown, so analyzing a malicious repo or opening a malicious ZIP runs arbitrary JavaScript in the studio origin and persists it. Separately, the in-browser parser regexes exhibit catastrophic backtracking (confirmed: 8 KB of a single identifier run freezes the main thread for ~272 s), so a single minified .js file in any analyzed repo hangs the tab. Loaded .openheart.json state files are consumed with zero schema validation, feeding more innerHTML sinks and attacker-chosen fetch URLs. Measured against the OWASP DOM XSS cheat sheet and Trusted Types, the app relies on ad-hoc, inconsistent escaping where a systemic sink-hardening control is needed. Also note five orphaned modules (app.js, ui.js, viewer.js, api.js, orb.js) are shipped but not loaded by index.html; viewer.js contains a latent raw innerHTML of third-party Kroki SVG that would be live XSS if ever wired up.
strengths: SVG card generators in uml-card-renderer.js consistently escapeXml() every interpolated value (name, fields, methods, instructions) and expose output only as inert data:image/svg+xml URIs used as Cytoscape background-image, so imported identifiers/comments cannot execute there.

The code viewer (editor.js) calls escapeHtml() on each source line before any regex syntax-highlighting, so raw markup inside analyzed source code is neutralized before reaching innerHTML — the editor is not an XSS sink.
File tree (file-tree.js) and breadcrumb updates use textContent/title for all file- and path-derived strings rather than innerHTML.
Default GitHub Pages deployment stores and transmits no GitHub token or credential — there is no secret to leak via URL, logs, or error messages.
The optional local Rust static-file server canonicalizes requested paths and verifies they stay under web/ (server.rs:258-272), blocking path traversal for static assets.
No analytics, trackers, or third-party beacons are embedded; privacy posture of the page itself is clean.

lens:TST.summary: Seen as a test suite, OpenHeart is broad but almost assertion-free where it matters. There are 76 tests: 47 unit tests, 36 of them in psa/, and 29 end-to-end runs. They exercise all 10 phases but check mostly counts, non-emptiness, string prefixes and counts that survive a write/read round trip, never analysis results against an oracle. That gap hides defects that reading the code confirms. SSA treats AST node indices as variable identity, so no φ or def-use edge is ever produced. Call resolution returns the enclosing method. `_ => Drop` deletes constructor bodies, and one test pins function_count == 2 for a fixture with three bodies. The .scpg file stores only counts. Faithful Python ports of the Rust code (exact re-implementations) show BP LCA wrong on 62% of random queries. BDD apply also contains unsound unsafe code that has never run under Miri. The HTTP server, CLI, exporter content and 9K lines of web JS have no tests at all. The F1 = 1.0 claim comes from a Python harness outside CI that compares a regex oracle with heuristic output after excluding problem class names. Genuinely good: the Rust tests are hermetic (tempdir only; no network, no shared state, no timing), several cross-phase hash-link and structural invariants are real, and a few unit tests are meaningful. A port of the Cooper dominator algorithm also matched a naive oracle on 3,000 random graphs. Reaching benchmark grade needs a test architecture built around oracles: proptest invariants, differential tests, insta goldens, cargo-fuzz, end-to-end runs on pinned repositories, and a cargo-mutants gate.
strengths: Integration tests are hermetic: every pipeline test writes into tempfile::tempdir(), with no dependence on network, target_repos/, the current directory or timing. They are fast and reproducible.

End-to-end coverage spans all 10 phases with realistic multi-file Java fixtures, and some cross-phase links are genuinely checked: ssa.cfa_hash == crc64(cfa bytes), cga.ssa_hash, psa.cfa_hash, and UMLLink scpg_hash == tra hash.

Several meaningful checks exist: the jump-table involution and parent<child ordering on a real parse, ROBDD canonicity over serialized node arrays, unique-table reduction rules, Pass1 discovery on a synthetic AST, Pass5 cycle rejection, structural Singleton detection, and #SAT((x1|x2)&x3) == 3.
Binary-layout tests (TokenRecord 16 B, SourceFileRecord 64 B, ROBDDNode 12 B, FunctionPSAHeader 32 B) guard the on-disk formats against accidental layout drift.

Some core algorithms are right, just unverified. A faithful Python port of compute_idom_cooper and reverse_postorder matched a naive dominator oracle on 3,000 random graphs, compute_post_idom is wired correctly, and ingestion's crc64_ecma matches the CRC-64/ECMA-182 check value 0x6C40DF5F0B497347.
Reusable fixtures already exist for golden and precision tests: examples/test_patterns_codebase (57 Java files labelled by pattern directory) and the committed web/diagrams/* outputs.

lens:LANG.summary: Seen through the language lens, OpenHeart is a Java analyzer with a partial JavaScript side path. Kotlin is lexed with the Java grammar and then re-parsed with the JavaScript grammar. Python, TypeScript, Rust, C++, Go, Swift and C# all go silently through tree-sitter-javascript, because Cargo.toml has only two grammars and both registries fall back to the JavaScript adapter. What looks like multi-language support is a layer of global token heuristics: keyword-then-capitalised-identifier sweeps and a 188-name blocklist. Those heuristics also corrupt Java output: `var` locals become fields, and generic bounds become supertypes. The F1 = 1.0000 claims come from a benchmark that scores only class names, and its regex oracle shares the engine's heuristics and most of its blocklist. Phases 3 to 9 never read the stored language id and hardcode JVM semantics: the Java semantic adapter and stubs, package-private defaults, invokevirtual-style dispatch, and allocation only through `new`. Import and package handling is effectively dead, and relations are joined back together by simple name. The good parts are real, though. Tree-sitter node-kind strings never leak past the adapter modules. Phases 7 to 10 use only the symbol, CFG, SSA and call-graph outputs. The Keep/Eliminate/Drop reduction and token-id anchoring are language-neutral ideas, and per-file language ids are already saved, so the right seams exist. Getting to state of the art needs five things: a language-neutral IR where each node is labelled with its role (Joern/Semgrep/CodeQL style); per-language lowering and semantics profiles; scope-graph name binding; one registry with real grammars; and an independent per-language benchmark. Until then the README, the API and the changelog should claim Java only.
strengths: Tree-sitter node-kind strings are confined to the adapter modules (src/ingestion/adapter, src/ast/adapter); a search finds none in Phases 3-10.
Phases 7-10 never reference AST node kinds; they consume only symbol, CFG, SSA and call-graph artifacts, which is a clean seam for a future language-neutral IR.
The Keep/Eliminate/Drop reduction contract (src/ast/adapter/mod.rs:10-21) and monotonic token-id anchoring are language-neutral concepts that carry over directly to a unified IR.

The language id is already saved per file in the .tca SourceFileRecord (src/core/types/source.rs:11-12). Trait seams (LanguageAdapter, ASTReductionAdapter, SemanticAdapter, CSTParser) already exist and could grow into a real frontend interface.
The Java reduction adapter covers most Java statement and expression kinds, including records, switch expressions, lambdas and method references.

find:BDD.summary: Phases 7 and 8 are a clearly documented skeleton. Some of the local mechanics are sound, but the semantics and the scaling are not yet benchmark-grade. What is genuinely good: make_node enforces both reduction rules, the apply/restrict terminal logic is right, and sat_count handles level gaps and variables above the root correctly (a faithful Python port matched brute-force model counts). The Phase 7 backward indexes are dense O(1) arrays, and the binary formats are compact and checksummed. The core problems are serious. The BDD library reads freed memory whenever its node Vec reallocates inside apply/restrict. The Phi_b encoding makes #SAT overstate real path counts by up to 11 orders of magnitude (21 guard-clause paths reported as 8.7e12). The FORCE/DFS variable orders blow up exponentially on plain sequential if/else, with no node or time budget, and the max-path DFS is exponential. 'Rudell sifting' is a no-op, the feasibility filter is unsound, and recursion handling is just a constant. In Phase 7, forward and navigation queries are linear scans despite the O(1) claim. The 'hash chain' hashes file counts and mtimes rather than artifact bytes, and incremental invalidation is dead code or a stub. Measured against CUDD/Sylvan/oxidd (complement edges, persistent computed tables, GC, dynamic reordering, budgets), Ball-Larus/KLEE-style path counting with SMT feasibility, and Kythe/SCIP/Salsa, the area is at prototype level, and the tautological 'theorem' tests cannot catch any of this. Four changes would help most: adopt oxidd or biodivine-lib-bdd, replace #SAT path counting with Ball-Larus dynamic programming over BigUint, add resource budgets, and rebuild traceability on stable, occurrence-based keys with per-entity content hashes.
strengths: UniqueTable::make_node enforces both ROBDD reduction rules in one place (lo==hi elimination, (var,lo,hi) sharing), the apply/restrict terminal cases are correct, and a debug-mode canonicity check exists.
sat_count correctly accounts for skipped levels and for variables above the root through its depth bookkeeping; a faithful port matched brute-force model counts on every tested function.
The Phase 7 backward indexes (BI_ast, BI_sym, BI_blk, BI_cs) are dense arrays indexed by entity id, giving genuine O(1) entity-to-token lookup.

The binary layouts are compact and fixed-width (12-byte ROBDD nodes, 32-byte PSA directory entries sorted by sym_id for binary search, 24-byte UMLLinks), with magic numbers, CRC checks and round-trip tests.
Clear phase decomposition with detailed specs (docs/plans/phase7.md, phase8.md); per-function ROBDD builds are independent, so fixes and parallelization can land locally.

find:SCPG.summary: Phase 10 is the least mature layer of OpenHeart compared with what the project claims for it. The "unified" .scpg holds ten element counts plus the string table. It is loaded with fs::read rather than mmap, its CRC-32 and version are never checked on load, a crafted 392-byte file crashes the loader, and no query reads the file. The query engine falls short of its names. Its "CFL-reachability" is a plain BFS over the call graph with an O(V·E) inner loop. Its "slice" is a closure over callers and parent symbols that ignores the def-use and CDG data the pipeline already builds, and it drops nodes under the depth limit. The incremental engine only XORs a constant into the hash, and doing that twice restores the old hash. Five compiler-IR diagrams (CFG, DFG, CDG, call graph, ROBDD) and several UML views are hard-coded templates or made-up content. The JSON IR invents file names and line numbers. The published gallery in web/diagrams was edited by hand rather than generated. Exporters identify classes by their simple name and emit some invalid PlantUML and Mermaid. Their output changes between runs, and the same logic is copied three or four times. XMI is a placeholder with numbered class names. What is genuinely good: strict identifier sanitization blocks injection, and the PlantUML class and package exporters are deterministic and model UML relationship kinds properly. The upstream artifacts (CSR call graph with SCCs, DefUseCSR, CDGCSR, TRA dense indexes) already hold what a real engine needs. Reaching the level of Joern, CodeQL or Glean needs four things: a real mmap container that carries content, an SDG/IFDS query layer, one diagram IR with validated printers, and test and benchmark infrastructure.
strengths: Explicit little-endian encoding, a fixed 128-byte header with magic, and a section directory with offset, length and CRC (src/scpg/serializer/mod.rs:141-165) are a reasonable skeleton for a real container format.

Identifier sanitization to letters, digits and underscore (plantuml.rs:211-227, mermaid.rs:522-540) makes PlantUML/Mermaid injection (@enduml, !include, quotes, newlines) practically impossible. JSON goes through serde, so its escaping is correct.

The PlantUML class and package exporters build nested package trees with BTreeMap and sort their dependency edges (plantuml.rs:372-506, 723-765). Those views are deterministic and keep generalization, realization, aggregation, composition and nesting distinct.
Mermaid activity diagrams render the real UMA ActivityEdge control flow rather than a template (mermaid.rs:1143-1162).

Upstream artifacts already contain what a real engine needs: CSR caller/callee adjacency plus SCCs in .cga (core/types/cg.rs:150-156), DefUseCSR and CDGCSR per function in .ssa, and dense bi_sym/sym_span indexes in .tra. The gap is wiring, not missing data.

find:UML.summary: Phase 9 is far from benchmark grade. Only the class records, the activity records and the sequence message lists come from real program facts, and even these drop most UML semantics: multiplicity, collection element types, guards, combined fragments and call nesting. Of the 14 advertised diagrams, seven are templated or hard-coded by the exporters, all labeled '100% Symbol-Grounded' and verified:true. Examples: timing tracks that describe OpenHeart itself, Uninitialized/Active state machines with invented onInit/executeWork/cleanup actions, and use cases taken from the first 3 methods of the first 6 classes. GoF detection is name and keyword matching plus a relation-filter bug that flags nearly every class with a field as Decorator and Composite. A re-implementation of the rules over the repo's own 35-class GoF corpus gives about 0.24 precision and 0.67 recall, with no roles, no calibrated scores and 11 of 23 patterns, far behind similarity-scoring and constraint-based detectors (Tsantalis 2006, DeMIMA, PINOT, DPDf) evaluated on P-MARt and DPB. The README's F1 = 1.0 is circular, because the oracle excludes the same blacklisted names the extractor drops, and it covers class names only; tests assert non-emptiness rather than roles or relationships. What is genuinely good: a compact, traceable record model with per-class UMLLinkRecords and CRC-checked artifacts, real inheritance and realization edges, CFG-backed activity skeletons, call-graph-backed messages with call-site tokens, and a clean pluggable exporter and visitor architecture that a rigorous engine can slot into.
strengths: Compact, typed binary record model (src/uma/types.rs) with a per-class UMLLinkRecord and CRC-64-checked .uma output: a sound base for source-to-diagram traceability.
Generalization and realization edges come from real type-hierarchy facts (sta.th_edges), with correct interface/abstract/enum/record stereotypes and UML visibility markers.
Activity records faithfully mirror the real CFG (blocks, edges, back-edges, PSA cyclomatic numbers), and sequence messages come from resolved call-graph edges that carry call-site tokens.
Pluggable exporter strategies (register/unregister per diagram type) and the UMAVisitor API let rigorous extractors replace the current ones without touching consumers.

The right structural ideas already exist in dead code: the symbol-phase Singleton check (src/symbol/uml_meta/patterns.rs) and Phase 3's AssociationDetector with aggregation/composition kinds and multiplicities can be revived.

find:CORE.summary: Phases 1 and 2 work as a prototype for Java only. They are not a benchmark-grade front end. The good parts are real: clean adapter seams (Keep/Eliminate/Drop), explicit little-endian I/O with one unsafe call, a correct CRC-64/ECMA-182, an interner that compares bytes so hash collisions never merge strings, and deterministic file and token ordering. The gaps against the state of the art are fundamental. Only Java gets a real grammar: Kotlin is lexed with the Java grammar and reduced with the JavaScript one, and every other language falls back to JavaScript. Within Java, the reducer's default Drop throws away constructor bodies, switch bodies, try-with-resources and generic types without any warning. The 'succinct' tree is the opposite of succinct: about 209 B/node in memory, mostly an O(n log n) sparse-table RMQ and a 32-bit jump table, against roughly 2–3 bits/node for an rmM-tree in sdsl-lite or vers-vecs. Its select is a 512-bit linear scan with a boundary bug, and LCA returns the wrong node for most queries. The artifact formats are not zero-copy and not reproducible (they embed timestamps). They are only partly validated and are hard-capped by u16/u8 fields (65,535 files or columns, 256 blocks per method). Ingestion runs on one thread and reads each file three times and parses it twice. No property tests, fuzzers or benchmarks back the README's compression, O(1) or F1 numbers. Getting to state of the art takes current tree-sitter with real grammars and complete node-type coverage, an rmM-tree, validated and aligned formats, single-pass parallel incremental ingestion, and a measurement harness.
strengths: Explicit little-endian encoding throughout (to_le_bytes/from_le_bytes) with no transmutes or pointer casts; the only unsafe in scope is the memmap2 call at src/core/io/mmap.rs:15.
StringInterner compares bytes when hashes match (src/ingestion/interner.rs:67), so FNV-1a collisions never merge strings; text_ids follow insertion order, which keeps them deterministic.

The CRC-64/ECMA-182 implementation is correct (it reproduces the check value 0x6C40DF5F0B497347). TokenCorpusSerializer::read checks CRC, magic and version and uses read_exact, so a truncated file returns Err instead of panicking.

Clean extension seams: the LanguageAdapter and ASTReductionAdapter traits with Keep/Eliminate/Drop decisions and LangId-keyed registries, plus fixed record layouts guarded by size tests (src/core/types/source.rs:66, src/core/types/token.rs:163).

Paths are sorted before file_ids are assigned and token_ids increase in source order; Phase 2's parsing of the .tca is bounds-checked, and the builder only ever emits balanced BP (the jump-table inverse invariant is tested).

find:SYM.summary: Phase 3 is a prototype, not a Java name-resolution engine. Its only real resolution is a name-only lexical walk over single-identifier type references, and most of what that walk needs is unavailable. The Phase 2 Java adapter drops it: imports, generic, array and qualified types, enum constants, constructor bodies and probably modifiers. What is left is rebuilt by token-window heuristics that misname annotated members, every parameter and long class headers. Cross-file resolution effectively does not exist: imports never arrive, would be mis-parsed and made global if they did, and imported or same-package types become simple-name SK_EXTERNAL placeholders that downstream exporters re-match by name. Supertypes and associations come from more token scans, which turn type arguments, bounds and Kotlin property types into supertypes, and a constant-true check makes every field an aggregation. Several loops are quadratic, the .sta bytes are non-deterministic, the containment tree is corrupted for any multi-file project, and the invariants repair the data they claim to check. Against javac Attr/Resolve, Eclipse JDT, JavaParser SymbolSolver, Spoon or scip-java, it lacks kind-directed lookup, JLS 6.4.1 import shadowing, inherited-member and overload resolution, a real JDK/classpath model, stable symbol identities and any ground-truth oracle; the advertised F1 counts only class names. What is genuinely good is the skeleton: fixed-width records, a clean five-pass structure behind a SemanticAdapter trait, panic-free iterative code, and a sound target spec in docs/plans/phase3.md that the code does not yet implement.
strengths: Fixed-width little-endian records (64-byte SymbolRecord, 32-byte ScopeRecord) with a CRC-64 trailer give a good base for an mmap-able, columnar .sta.
The five-pass decomposition (discovery, imports, types, members, hierarchy) sits behind a SemanticAdapter trait, which is the right seam for per-language adapters.
Phase 3 code is iterative and bounds-checked, and I found no panic path on realistic input: lookup_text handles u32::MAX, and all token indexing is guarded.
docs/plans/phase3.md sets the right target: scope graphs with parent and import edges, JLS-ordered resolution with an explicit SK_EXTERNAL fallback, and an assoc_kind decision table.
Unresolved references become explicit SK_EXTERNAL symbols with interned qualified names instead of being dropped. That is the right instinct; it needs FQNs and reason codes.

find:FLOW.summary: Phases 4-6 are a prototype scaffold. The data structures and a few kernels follow the literature: CSR graphs, RPO-renumbered blocks, Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy dominator and dominance-frontier code (a Python port of each matched a naive reference on 3,000 random CFGs), a textbook Cytron/renaming skeleton, and Tarjan SCC. The semantic layers on top of them mostly do not work for real Java. The CFG builder never connects try and do-while statements, so they and all code after them are pruned. It also picks loop children by position (losing most enhanced-for bodies), has no exceptional edges, finally semantics, labels or synchronized handling, and inherits a Phase 2 reduction that drops switch bodies, constructor bodies and try-with-resources. A silent sink→EXIT patch hides all of this from the invariants. SSA keys variables by AST-node occurrence, so no φ-function or def-use edge is ever produced. The CDG walks the wrong adjacency and returns the CFG edge set, and the 'IFDS solver' is a three-predicate syntactic stub. The call graph resolves almost every call to its own enclosing method; CHA matches by name only and walks downward only; 'Andersen' has no real constraints and mixes per-function SSA ids. Phase 6 is quadratic in symbols × call sites, every graph walk is recursive (a crash risk for the single-threaded server), the CFG/DFG/CDG/CG diagrams users see are hard-coded templates, and the tests pass on these defects and in places encode them. This is far from parity with Soot/SootUp, WALA, OPAL, Doop, Joern or PhASAR. The realistic path is a typed IR or bytecode front end, symbol-resolved SSA (Braun et al. 2013), a JLS-faithful CHA→RTA→points-to call graph and a real RHS tabulation solver, validated on CATS, Judge and DaCapo.
strengths: compute_idom_cooper is a correct Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy implementation: a faithful Python port matched naive dominator sets on 3,000 random CFGs (self-loops, irreducible regions, unreachable nodes), and RPO renumbering keeps idom/DF arrays dense.

The dominance-frontier runner algorithm (frontier.rs) is correct and deterministic: the port matched the textbook DF definition on 3,000 random CFGs with a predecessor-free ENTRY, and output lists are sorted.
Compact CSR encodings are used for CFG successors/predecessors, DF, def-use, CDG and the callee/caller CG, with CRC-64 checksums and hash links to upstream artifacts: a good mmap-friendly base.

The SSA skeleton is textbook: Cytron worklist φ placement with a pruning hook, dominator-tree renaming with version stacks, and φ arguments filled from successors. With symbol-resolved variables it is close to working, and postdom.rs's unused compute_post_idom is a correct reverse-graph formulation.

Tarjan's SCC is algorithmically correct, with self- versus mutual-recursion classification, and each phase asserts explicit invariants (unique EXIT, idom completeness, φ arity, CSR consistency, SCC coverage). That is the right habit; the checks just need to be stronger.

find:SRV.summary: This surface is a prototype wearing production language, and against axum/hyper/tower-http and OWASP ASVS it is far from benchmark-grade. The hand-rolled server in server.rs has three independent critical holes reachable in the default 0.0.0.0 deployment: /api/source reads arbitrary files by using the decoded query value directly as a path (plus a basename walkdir fallback), and /api/analyze shells out to `git clone` on an unvalidated, attacker-controlled URL (SSRF, git argument injection, non-https transports, repo-name traversal, unbounded disk, no cleanup) while the written validate_url is dead code that itself panics on `owner`-only URLs. The HTTP layer is not spec-compliant: Content-Length is ignored, the body is one 8 KiB read plus a conditional 4 KiB read gated on the substring "repo_url", a 500 ms read timeout truncates real requests, HEAD returns a body, and the single-threaded serial accept loop running the full 10-phase pipeline (and a network clone) per request makes a one-line DoS trivial. CORS `*` with no auth lets any website drive these endpoints and exfiltrate local files cross-origin. Deployment is broken and unhardened: the Docker CMD invokes a `serve --port` subcommand the CLI does not implement, so the documented container exits immediately; the image runs as root with no healthcheck, a `|| true` that hides build failures, and no .dockerignore; release CI ships a .rlib instead of the binary. Documentation overstates reality: advertised env knobs (RUST_LOG, OPENHEART_MAX_MEMORY_MB, OPENHEART_NUM_THREADS, OPENHEART_STRICT_INVARIANTS) are read nowhere, the claimed `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` appears in no file, and SECURITY.md lists 1.0.x/1.1.x versions that do not exist for a 0.1.0 crate. What is genuinely good: the non-API static file route does canonicalize and confine under web/ (the one correct security control here), JSON string values are escaped before interpolation, artifact deserializers verify CRC-64 and check a minimum length before parsing, the pipeline module structure is clean, and dependency hygiene via Dependabot plus a pinned Cargo.lock is sound. The fix is not incremental: replace the custom server with axum/hyper behind tower-http (timeouts, body/concurrency limits, CORS allowlist), sandbox or remove server-side cloning, and move the CLI to clap.
strengths: The non-API static-file route (server.rs:254-286) canonicalizes the requested path and rejects anything not under canonicalize("web") — the single correct path-traversal defense in the file, and the model the /api/source route should have followed.
JSON responses escape backslash, quote, and control characters via a dedicated closure (server.rs:701-707) before interpolating user/file data, avoiding naive JSON-injection in the analyze response.

Artifact deserializers (e.g. uma/serializer.rs:230-240, tra/serializer.rs:114-120) verify a CRC-64/ECMA checksum and check a minimum length before trusting header fields, giving real tamper-detection on binary inputs.
Dependency supply chain is reasonably maintained: Cargo.lock is committed and pinned, Dependabot watches cargo and github-actions weekly/monthly, and recent commits are dependency bumps.
Clean separation of the 10 pipeline phases into focused modules keeps the engine itself readable and testable even though the adapter layer wrapping it is weak.

find:WEB.summary: The web studio is not benchmark-grade yet. It does have real strengths: the navigation code is careful (wheel deltaMode normalisation, a trackpad-pinch fast path, rAF-coalesced panning, animation loops that stop when they settle), and SVG card text is escaped consistently. The worst problems are about trust, not polish. On GitHub Pages the only analyzer that actually runs is a regex scanner over the first 30 files. It assigns members to the wrong classes, turns method calls into methods, makes same-named classes collide on node id, and can freeze the tab through cubic backtracking. 13 of the 19 projections, the source shown for unresolved files, the traceability line highlights and the 'SCPG ... Verified' badges are made up. The real Rust engine is almost never used, because the client gives up after 2.5 s and ignores the response. Security is weak: file names from analysed repos, ZIP entry names and shared state files reach innerHTML with no CSP or SRI, which gives DOM XSS on a github.io origin shared by all the owner's Pages sites. Layout is grid packing rather than layered layout: the landing class diagram is a 1,942x16,000 px column and the sequence diagram is one 20,900 px row. There is also no level-of-detail rendering, Web Worker offloading, IR validation, accessibility layer, tests, linter or CI gate. Compared with Mermaid Live, the PlantUML server, Excalidraw/tldraw or Sourcetrail the gap is foundational. It needs a real parser (tree-sitter or the Rust engine compiled to WASM), elkjs, a document model with undo, a strict CSP and a tested build before new features are added.
strengths: SVG card generators escape all text with escapeXml (web/js/uml-card-renderer.js:712-719), and the file tree and logger use textContent, so the canvas rendering itself is not an XSS sink.

Navigation is well engineered: deltaMode normalisation, trackpad-pinch fast path, rAF-coalesced drag panning, and zoom/pan animation loops that stop on convergence (web/js/graph-canvas.js:824-1019). The minimap viewfinder moves with GPU transforms (web/js/minimap-navigator.js:552-573).

Relationship notation and colours come from the manifest (web/js/themes/theme-manager.js:126-164), and theme tokens live in CSS variables. Light and dark themes are supported, defaulting to prefers-color-scheme.
No secrets or tokens are persisted. The codebase is dependency-light ES modules, and every file passes node --check.

There is a working undo/redo foundation that coalesces each drag into one action and keeps toolbar state in sync (web/js/graph-canvas.js:2073-2139, 2257-2330). The LLM-oriented structure export is a distinctive idea.

find:ENG.summary: This area is at early-prototype maturity, well short of rust-analyzer, ruff, Biome, Joern or Semgrep practice, and the biggest problem is that the documentation promises far more than the code delivers. The code contradicts the headline claims. Kotlin is tokenized with the Java grammar and reduced with the JavaScript grammar. The other four advertised languages (Python, Rust, TypeScript, C++) fall back to JavaScript. 'F1 = 1.0000' comes from a regex-vs-regex class-name check that strips a hand-tuned blacklist from both sides. '128x' is a theoretical bound (the project's own overview says 6.9x), 'O(1)' navigation is a linear scan, and the incremental, IFDS, CFL, LSP and XMI features marked complete are stubs or missing. Testing is mostly smoke-level: two tautologies, plus checks for non-emptiness, serializer round-trips and text prefixes. There is no property, differential, fuzz, snapshot, mutation or coverage testing, and an unsafe aliasing use-after-free in the BDD core has gone unnoticed for lack of Miri. CI runs only check, fmt and test on Linux. The release workflow has never run, and the Dockerfile can neither build nor start. Artifacts embed wall-clock time, so neither the hash chain nor any golden test can reproduce. Across the architecture, errors are strings or panics, the 10-phase wiring is copied at 18 call sites, everything is public, and nothing runs in parallel. What is genuinely good: a clean phase/artifact decomposition with a hash-chain design, deterministic exporter output, a handful of precise unit tests, basic Dependabot/rustfmt hygiene, and the instinct to use external ground truth. The fastest route to credibility is to retract or footnote unbacked claims now, then build a pinned-corpus accuracy and performance harness and a CI gate stack (clippy, MSRV, Miri, cargo-fuzz, proptest, insta, llvm-cov, cargo-deny) before adding features.
strengths: Clean phase decomposition into versioned, magic-tagged binary artifacts with an explicit cross-phase hash-chain design and serializer round-trip tests: a solid skeleton for caching and incremental analysis once serialization is made deterministic.

Some genuinely precise tests exist: a hand-built diamond CFG with exact idom and dominance-frontier expectations (tests/cfg_tests.rs:103-128), symbol-builder kind/parent checks (tests/symbol_tests.rs:136-142), record-layout size assertions (src/core/types/token.rs:162-165), and 40 focused BDD unit tests.

Exporter output is deliberately deterministic: BTreeMap package trees and sorted, deduplicated PlantUML optimizer output (src/scpg/diagram/export/plantuml.rs:650-655, plantuml_optimizer.rs:116-118). That makes insta snapshot testing cheap to add.

Baseline hygiene is present: committed Cargo.lock, Dependabot for cargo and GitHub Actions, rustfmt enforced in CI, a beta-toolchain canary, SECURITY.md, a code of conduct, issue/PR templates, and a Keep-a-Changelog format.

The benchmark scripts reach for real external ground truth: iluwatar/java-design-patterns .urm.puml files and spring-petclinic. This is the right instinct; it needs pinned commits, fully qualified names, relation scoring and CI integration.

lens:SCALE.summary: Through this lens, OpenHeart is a prototype that has only been run on corpora of a few hundred lines (the largest in-repo example is 451 LOC), and it would not finish on a 1M-LOC Java codebase. Phase 8's longest-path DFS is exponential in sequential branches (exactly 4·2^k pops in a model of the code), Phase 6 does full symbol-table scans per call site per AST ancestor (~10^13 record visits), Phase 9 rebuilds a global edge map per entry point, and Phase 3 resolves cross-file types with an O(R·S) scan. The memory claims are contradicted: the 'succinct' AST costs about 210–236 B/node (≈1.1 GB at 5M nodes) because of an O(n log n) sparse table, and the 'unified mmap' .scpg file stores only counts. Unbounded recursion on the 1 MB Windows main thread, u16/u8 id widths and a single-threaded synchronous server let large or adversarial inputs crash or hang the service. There is no parallelism, every file is parsed twice, every log level is written unbuffered to two files, and there is neither incremental reuse nor a benchmark harness that could have caught any of this. The building blocks are genuinely good: packed sort keys, CSR adjacency, dense backward indexes, Cooper–Harvey–Kennedy dominators and flat artifacts. Most fixes are standard (O(N) index maps, iterative traversals, DAG dynamic programming, rayon per file and per function). After them, ruff/rust-analyzer-class front-end throughput and SootUp/OPAL-class CHA call-graph times are plausible.
strengths: Phase 7 backward indexes (src/tra/backward/*.rs) are dense, id-indexed arrays built in linear time, so id→source-span lookup really is O(1).

Pass 1 declaration discovery (src/symbol/passes/pass1_discovery.rs:106-194) is a single non-recursive preorder sweep using parent_map plus per-node symbol/scope arrays. It is the O(N) pattern the later phases should copy.

Packed (file, line, col) u64 sort keys and an open-addressing FNV-1a interner (src/ingestion/interner.rs) keep token storage compact and lookups simple. The flat little-endian artifact formats are a good substrate for zero-copy mmap and content-addressed caching.

Where the algorithms are used they are sound choices: CSR adjacency for CFG/CG, Cooper–Harvey–Kennedy dominators, a per-function BDD library with RPO+FORCE initial ordering, and capped FORCE and liveness iteration counts.

Some indexes are already built correctly and show the fix pattern: Phase 8's sym_id→index HashMaps (src/psa/mod.rs:83-96), class_diagram's children_map, and the minimap's edge sampling and cached canvases.

lens:E2E.summary: Through the end-to-end lens, OpenHeart is a clean 10-phase skeleton whose phases rarely hand each other usable data. Several parts are genuinely good: typed per-phase artifact structs with magic, version and CRC framing; Result propagation through Phases 1-6 in the CLI; deterministic file-id assignment; a real CSR CFG with Cooper dominators that actually drives the activity records; and per-file SHA-256 hashes that could key a cache. The seams everything depends on are broken, though. Call resolution returns the caller itself. SSA ignores the symbol table and keys variables by AST node. Kotlin is parsed by a different grammar in each phase. The five compiler-IR diagrams are hard-coded templates, and the API's design means Phase 4-8 data cannot reach them. IDs cross phases as bare u32 values and get reinterpreted (AST node as symbol, SSA id as BDD variable, name id as symbol). Outputs cannot be reproduced (timestamps, mtimes, HashMap order), traceability stops before the UI, and the .scpg 'database' stores counts instead of data. Four separate pipelines (CLI, server, test builder, browser regex engine) give different answers. The F1 = 1.0 harness excludes 184 of the 188 names the engine itself suppresses, and the integration tests contain tautologies. CodeQL uses content-keyed TRAP labels feeding one checked database; Joern builds one CPG id space through layered passes; rust-analyzer/Salsa uses interned stable ids and memoized queries with early cutoff. Measured against them, OpenHeart lacks one orchestrator, typed stable ids, a persisted queryable graph and golden end-to-end oracles. The benchmark claims cannot be backed up until those exist.
strengths: Clear phase decomposition with explicit artifact structs and per-phase binary serializers carrying magic, version and CRC-64: the right skeleton for provenance.
Phases 1-6 return Result, and cmd_analyze propagates failures with ? instead of continuing on empty data (src/main.rs:152-204).

Phase 1 sorts the manifest before assigning file ids (src/ingestion/mod.rs:38-39), and the server sorts discovered files (src/adapters/server.rs:486), so id assignment does not depend on directory-walk order.

Phase 4 builds real per-function CSR CFGs with Cooper dominators and dominance frontiers, and the activity records are genuinely derived from those blocks and edges (src/uma/behavioral/activity_diagram.rs:49-120).
Per-file SHA-256 hashes and a source-tree hash are already computed in Phase 1 (src/ingestion/mod.rs:56-97), ready to key a content-addressed cache.

Some ordering hygiene exists: call sites and the points-to table are sorted (src/cg/call_sites.rs:66; src/cg/mod.rs:79), and the PlantUML package tree uses BTreeMap (src/scpg/diagram/export/plantuml.rs:376-379).
Every phase has integration and serialization round-trip tests, a base on which golden oracles can be layered.

lens:FIT.summary: Seen through the benchmark-integrity lens, OpenHeart's headline results do not show that it generalizes. The "F1 = 1.0000" claim compares simple class names against a regex oracle. That oracle shares a 184-name exclusion list with the tool (edited in the same commits), erases the tool's own placeholder phantoms before scoring and collapses duplicate names. For every non-Java language it compares two keyword scanners, because those languages are parsed with the JavaScript grammar. Five of the 19 advertised projections (CFG, DFG, CDG, call graph, ROBDD) are constant templates; the CDG literally hard-codes the paper's PaymentService example ("amount > 0", "repository.saveOrder()"). Most behavioral UML views, the XMI export and the whole GitHub Pages studio are built from fixed templates, random "verified" hashes, fixed timings and invented members and line numbers. GoF detection is keyed on class-name substrings while the structural detectors that exist are never called; the bundled Factory Method, Observer and Template Method examples are missed, and 6 of the 8 name-derived labels on the examples disappear under neutral renaming. The test and script suites are dominated by existence, syntax and round-trip checks, and several checks are hard-wired to pass, so none of this is caught. What is genuinely good: the Rust code contains no hard-coded example class names, a few tests use real hand-derived labels (dominators, #SAT, BDD canonicity), sequence diagrams really are derived from call-graph sites, artifacts are hash-chained with CRC-verified deserializers, and the verification scripts already have the right skeleton (explicit phantom/missing lists, an external .urm.puml oracle) for an honest harness.
strengths: No example or dataset class names are hard-coded in the Rust analysis code: grepping src/ for 35 identifiers from examples/, sample_codebase/ and the named datasets returns zero hits. The overfitting comes from name substrings, templates and the shared deny-list instead.

Some tests use genuine independent labels: hand-derived idom and dominance-frontier expectations (tests/cfg_tests.rs:120-128), #SAT = 3 for (x1 or x2) and x3 (tests/research_paper_theorems_tests.rs:82-84), ROBDD canonicity invariants (tests/psa_tests.rs:128-147), and BDD unit tests with hand-computed counts (src/psa/bdd/sat_count.rs:110-143).
Sequence diagrams are actually derived from analysis: SequenceDiagramExtractor walks cga.call_sites from fan-in-0 entry points (src/uma/behavioral/sequence_diagram.rs:86-140).
Artifacts are hash-chained and most deserializers verify CRC-64 (src/cfg/serializer.rs, src/ssa/serializer.rs, src/cg/serializer.rs and others), which is a sound basis for benchmark provenance.

ruthless_verify.py prints explicit phantom and missing lists, and scripts/benchmark_all_java_design_patterns.py already compares against an external oracle (.urm.puml) produced by a different tool. This is the right shape for an independent harness.

lens:ROB.summary: Through this lens OpenHeart is not yet safe to run on untrusted input, or even on large real-world code. The worst problems are cross-cutting. An unsound unsafe block in the BDD library reads freed memory on almost every function that has a branch. Phase 8 enumerates CFG paths exponentially, so protobuf-style methods with about 40 sequential ifs never finish. The HTTP server runs everything inline on its only thread, with no catch_unwind, no timeouts and no path confinement, so any panic, hang or crafted request becomes a remote kill or a file disclosure (/api/source?file=/etc/passwd, served with wildcard CORS). Packed u8/u16 fields (def_block, column, file_id, span lines) wrap silently at sizes benchmarks hit routinely. Overflow checks are off in every profile, and a single line longer than 64 KB aborts the analysis of a whole repository. Recursion depth is controlled by the input in more than ten walkers, and the artifact readers trust header counts behind a CRC that is not a security boundary. What is genuinely good: the analysis passes are mostly written defensively (bounds-checked .get() and len guards, saturating sat_count, guarded divisions), cyclic inheritance is sanitized instead of looping, phases 1-6 return Result, and the static-file route canonicalizes and confines paths correctly. The right patterns already exist in the codebase but are not applied everywhere, and nothing in CI (no fuzzing, no Miri, no overflow-checked build) would catch the gaps.
strengths: Most analysis passes guard indices defensively: pass1-5 token lookups check `< token_records.len()`, BPASTArtifact accessors return sentinels out of range, and DefUseCSR::uses_of validates offsets before slicing.
StringInterner::lookup_text is fully bounds-checked, and TokenCorpusSerializer::read uses a read_exact-based BinaryReader, so truncated .tca input fails with Err rather than a panic.
sat_count uses saturating shifts and multiplies (psa/bdd/sat_count.rs), and every division or modulo in src/ is by a constant or a guarded value.

Cyclic type hierarchies from malformed code are explicitly broken by sanitize_th_graph (symbol/builder.rs:162-226) instead of looping forever; the liveness and FORCE fixpoints are bounded (100 and 200 rounds).
Phases 1-6 return Result, and the CLI turns those errors into messages; artifacts carry CRC-64 checksums, which detect accidental corruption.
The static-file route correctly canonicalizes paths and confines them under web/ (server.rs:254-272), a pattern that can be reused for the other routes.

find2:SCPG.summary: This pass read every in-scope file top to bottom: src/scpg/mod.rs, types.rs, api/{mod,builder}.rs, serializer/{mod,integrity,layout}.rs, mmap/mod.rs, incremental/{mod,delta}.rs, query/{mod,cache,cfl,impact,navigation,robdd,slice}.rs, tests/scpg_tests.rs and tests/surgical_pipeline_dump_test.rs. It also checked them against docs/plans/phase10.md and against the upstream artifact types and the code that produces their hashes. It adds 38 items not in the first-round list. The biggest are: Phase 10 panics on I/O errors; scpg_hash changes on every run and has two incompatible definitions; the inputs' hash chain is never verified; source_hash is always zero; cache keys ignore the artifacts passed with each call; and test coverage has large gaps. All in-scope files were reviewed fully; src/scpg/diagram was excluded per the scope.
strengths: Header (128 B) and directory (24 B per entry) byte offsets agree between writer (serializer/mod.rs:141-165) and reader (mmap/mod.rs:26-72); all fields are fixed-size little-endian.
The CRC-32 routine is correct: the known-answer value 0xCBF43926 for '123456789' was verified with Python.
Slice and impact results are sorted before returning, so HashSet iteration order does not leak into the output.
QueryKey parameter packing (a<<32 | b) is collision-free within one query type, and the cache clears itself when scpg_hash changes.
MemoryMappedSCPG::open checks the minimum length and the magic before parsing, and get_section bounds-checks the end offset against the file length.
Section order lives in one place (SectionLayoutPlanner) and matches the documented hot/warm/cold classes.

find2:UML.summary: This second pass read every file in src/uma line by line: the structural, behavioral and pattern extractors, actor identification, label extraction, the visitors, the builder, the serializer, types and mod.rs. It also read the five test files in scope. To confirm real effects it cross-checked producers (symbol passes, CFG, call graph, AST adapter, ingestion) and consumers (the scpg exporters, the CLI and the server). Every file in scope was reviewed in full. While the review was running, another session added uncommitted edits to src/uma/types.rs and Cargo.toml in the working tree, so all line numbers refer to committed HEAD fc218cd. That is the same baseline the first-round list uses.
strengths: UMASerializer::read checks the magic and a CRC-64 over the whole payload before it parses any record.
Extraction is cleanly split into structural, behavioral and pattern modules. The UMAVisitor trait has default no-op methods, so new analyses are cheap to add.
Sibling-chain walks guard child_id < symbol_records.len(), and interner lookups are bounds-checked, so most traversal code cannot index out of range.
Sequence extraction pre-indexes call-site edges in a HashMap and keeps a visited set, so cyclic and recursive call graphs terminate.
Activity extraction reads the CFG after RPO compaction, so activity graphs contain no unreachable blocks and have exactly one exit.

find2:SCPGX.summary: This pass read every line of src/scpg/diagram (mod.rs, common.rs, factory.rs, renderers.rs, export/{mod,json,mermaid,plantuml,plantuml_optimizer,xmi}.rs). It also traced the UMA/STA records those files consume (sequence, activity and class builders, primitive and stub symbol ids, package symbols) to confirm what the exporters actually receive. The web/diagrams gallery was checked with a Python integrity script for duplicate ids, dangling edges, duplicate files and manifest kinds, plus spot reads. The large generated samples (sequence.puml 110KB, sequence/communication.json 144KB) were checked by script and spot reads, not line by line. No PlantUML or Mermaid renderer was available, so the syntax claims come from reading the code and are marked by confidence.
strengths: PlantUML class and package diagrams use BTreeMap and sorted dependency lists, so those parts of the output are stable across runs.
Identifiers pass through an alnum/underscore sanitizer before reaching PlantUML/Mermaid, and JSON is produced via serde, so source names cannot inject diagram directives.
Token and record lookups are bounds-checked; there are no panicking unwrap/expect calls on fallible input in this scope.
PlantUML and Mermaid strategy registries make diagram types pluggable, and tests exercise registration and removal.
Mermaid activity export keys nodes by function_sym_id and uses the real CFG edges from UMA.

find2:SRV.summary: This pass re-read every file in the SRV scope from top to bottom: server.rs, web_repo.rs, adapters/mod.rs, main.rs, Dockerfile, run.sh, run.bat, scripts/restart_server.sh, Makefile, .env.example, SECURITY.md and docs/security-architecture.md. It also checked the server against the ingestion adapters, the logger, the serializers and the web client that calls it, and left out the 16 items already reported. The new findings cover availability (git credential prompts, panics, symlink walks, no write timeout), clone-cache and file-discovery correctness, invalid hand-built JSON, CLI crashes and false inspect claims, and hazards in the launcher scripts; .env.example had nothing beyond SRV-14. Every file was reviewed in full. Three claims could not be run here (no toolchain, no batch test) and are marked medium confidence: Windows refusing to delete the mapped .tca, the Rust 1.80 MSRV breaking the Docker build, and cmd.exe parsing of run.bat.
strengths: Static file handler canonicalizes request paths and requires them to stay under web/ (src/adapters/server.rs:257-272), blocking classic ../ traversal.
git is spawned with an argv array, not through a shell, so shell metacharacters in repo_url cannot inject commands.
The /api/source success body is built with serde_json, so file content is escaped correctly.
The CLI pipeline propagates every phase failure with ? and phase-specific messages (src/main.rs:152-226).
collect_files sorts its output and ingestion re-sorts, so file ids are deterministic for a fixed file set.
cmd_inspect checks lengths before reading magic numbers (src/main.rs:357, 370).
web_repo.rs has unit tests for URL validation and the diagram-type count.

find2:BDD.summary: Second pass over every file in src/psa/** and src/tra/** and the three test files, read top to bottom at HEAD, with checks against the code that produces and consumes them (cfg, ssa, cg, server, scpg, uma). I ran a brute-force Python model of the exact Phi_b encoding (C:\Users\AHMAD_~1\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\D--Repos-OpenHeart\31873741-1e3a-46df-bb5d-a94a867cbe24\scratchpad\round2\bdd_model.py and loop_enum.py). For straight-line code, if/else and the psa_tests compute() method it gives sat_count = 2, 8 and 24, against true path counts of 1, 2 and 4, and it shows a loop assignment that never reaches EXIT but is still counted; this confirms BDD2-01 and BDD2-02. While I was reviewing, someone else started an uncommitted rewrite in the working tree: src/psa/bdd/{mod,apply,restrict,sat_count,unique_table}.rs and src/psa/ordering/mod.rs were modified, and bdd/library.rs, bdd/fxhash.rs and src/psa/count.rs were added. I did not review that in-progress work. All findings cite HEAD, and BDD2-04, -11, -13 to -16, -19 and -20 may already be addressed by it. Every in-scope HEAD file was reviewed fully.
strengths: UniqueTable::make_node applies both ROBDD reduction rules simply and correctly (elimination before lookup, then sharing).
restrict and sat_count are algorithmically correct on well-ordered BDDs; sat_count's depth propagation does account for leading free variables when called with depth = n_vars.
FORCE is deterministic (explicit index tie-break), and the RPO, longest-path and sifting node-count walks use explicit stacks.
The PSA reader checks magic and CRC before decoding; the header and metrics records have round-trip unit tests.
TRA symbol ids are positional and match STA allocation (symbol/builder.rs:67-69), so BI_sym and SymbolSpan addressing is consistent; the forward_sym_query containment logic is correct.
The module layout mirrors the spec sections, which makes spec-versus-code comparison straightforward.

find2:FLOW.summary: This pass covered every file in the FLOW scope from top to bottom: src/cfg/** (builder, stmts, analysis, serializer, mod), src/ssa/**, src/cg/**, src/core/types/{cfg,ssa,cg}.rs, and tests/{cfg,ssa,cg}_tests.rs. I opened the Java AST adapter, reducer, logger, TRA, PSA and UMA files only to confirm how they consume these phases. The 49 findings are all new relative to FLOW-01..21. Main ones: empty bodies wired to EXIT; SSA def/use extraction gaps; no entry definitions; nondeterministic φ numbering; lambda self-loops; call_site_id/position mismatch; a latent CGCSR::edges_of panic; and a .cga pre-allocation DoS. Every in-scope file was reviewed in full, but only by reading the code: no Rust toolchain was available, so nothing was compiled or run.
strengths: Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy idom (dominators.rs) and Cytron dominance frontiers (frontier.rs) are implemented correctly for reducible CFGs. Renumbering blocks into RPO keeps the iteration simple.
The pruned-SSA design is textbook: liveness-gated φ placement with phi_placed/defsites guards, then dominator-tree renaming with version stacks.
Successors, predecessors, DF, def-use, CDG and call-graph adjacency all use compact CSR layouts with bounds-checked accessors (get_succs, uses_of).
Tarjan SCC (scc.rs) is correct and separates self-recursive from mutually recursive components.
postdom.rs has a correct reverse-graph post-dominator, which could replace the CDG's own version.
Artifacts carry CRC-64 checksums and upstream link hashes. Points-to, CHA targets and IFDS outputs are sorted for deterministic output.

find2:SYM.summary: This pass reviewed every tracked file in scope from top to bottom: the 19 files under src/symbol, src/core/types/symbol.rs and tests/symbol_tests.rs. It also traced effects into the AST reducer, interner, logger and exporters, and found 44 issues not in the first-round list. The worst are packages truncated at segments like `data`, primitive and JDK types missing from .sta (so diagram member types print blank), implements clauses recorded as extends edges, every declarator duplicated as a local, the token sweep turning parameters into classes, and constructor bodies dropped before Phase 3. Citations are against HEAD fc218cd. During the review someone began editing the working tree: core/io/binary.rs, core/types/ast.rs and scpg/diagram/common.rs were modified, and untracked files src/symbol/ast_index.rs and src/symbol/model.rs appeared, not yet wired into mod.rs. I did not audit those two files. Findings that rest on tree-sitter-java 0.20.2 node names (constructor_body, switch_block, `var` parsed as a type_identifier) were checked against my knowledge of the grammar, not local sources, and carry medium confidence.
strengths: SymbolRecord (64 B) and ScopeRecord (32 B) are fixed size, serialized field by field in explicit little-endian order and protected by a CRC-64 trailer, so .sta is portable and detects corruption.
Core accessors (SymbolTableBuilder::symbol, the BPASTArtifact accessors, StringInterner::lookup_text) are bounds-checked, so most passes return None or empty instead of panicking on bad ids.
The five-pass structure with a SemanticAdapter trait gives a clean seam for per-language semantics.
Package symbols are de-duplicated by full path, and package names are exposed per symbol and per file for downstream exporters.
Type-hierarchy edges are de-duplicated on insert, and acyclicity is checked with Kahn's algorithm before the artifact is built.

find2:CORE.summary: This second pass read every file in scope from top to bottom, with no compilation: src/core (mod, io/binary, io/mmap, logger, pipeline, types/*), all of src/ingestion and src/ast including the parser and adapter submodules, tests/ingestion_tests.rs and tests/ast_tests.rs. Struct layouts, the CRC-64 check value and the TCA magic byte order were checked with Python. The main new problems are in the Java reducer mappings: declarators duplicate declarations, enum constants are dropped, many other constructs are discarded, and the AST stores no child roles, so CFG loop decoding goes wrong. Other new items are a latent CGCSR panic, panicking late phases behind a Result API, unverified hash links, plus many smaller robustness, performance, documentation and test gaps. All files in scope were reviewed fully.
strengths: Phases have clear module boundaries, with per-language adapter traits for both tokenization and CST reduction.
Both binary formats end in a CRC-64/ECMA-182 trailer (check value verified), and the core token and file records have size_of layout tests.
Phase 1 checks sort-key injectivity and per-file token completeness before serializing.
File order is deterministic (paths are sorted before assigning file ids), so sort keys are stable for a given input set.
Most BP AST accessors bounds-check their indices instead of panicking, and the string interner has amortized resize and dedup.

find2:WEB.summary: This second pass read every file in scope from top to bottom: index.html, app.js, all of web/js including themes, manifest.json and both theme CSS files, plus deploy_pages.yml. It checked the regexes in Node, compared the bundled diagram JSON in Python, and computed WCAG contrast ratios. Main new problems: PNG export always throws a ReferenceError, Java heritage parsing gives wrong inheritance edges, Kotlin classes, records and Kotlin packages are not detected, ROBDD and state-machine terminals render wrong, and several real UX, accessibility and robustness bugs. Not reviewed line by line: style.css lines 1000-1740 (scanned with greps), the prose and SVG of web/docs/*.html (checked for structure, scripts and algorithm claims only), the orphaned modules (ui.js, viewer.js, api.js, orb.js; read lightly), and the diagrams/*.json data other than manifest.json (sampled programmatically).
strengths: uml-card-renderer.js escapes every interpolated string with escapeXml before building SVG data URIs
graph-loader.js drops edges whose endpoints are missing, so a bad IR does not crash Cytoscape
Theme pub/sub (theme-manager.js applyTheme) isolates listener errors with try/catch
file-tree.js builds rows with textContent rather than innerHTML for file names
Undo/redo is a clean command-pattern stack with a bounded history (maxHistory 50)
Minimap viewfinder updates are rAF-throttled and use GPU transforms instead of redrawing the thumbnail
sessionStorage writes of the custom codebase are wrapped in try/catch with a console warning

find2:ENG.summary: This second pass over the ENG scope covered Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock, the Makefile, the .github workflows, dependabot config and templates, every Python and shell script under scripts/, ruthless_verify.py and its config, the dot-config files, README, ROADMAP, CHANGELOG, docs/** and examples/README.md. It found 59 new items. Line numbers refer to HEAD fc218cd. While I was reviewing, someone made uncommitted edits to .editorconfig, .gitattributes, .gitignore, Cargo.toml, Makefile and README.md in the working tree, and these may already fix parts of ENG2-39, ENG2-40 and ENG2-41. I reviewed the following through headings, targeted sections and scripted checks rather than line by line: docs/plans/phase3.md and phase5-9.md, the 12 HTML specs and docs/openheart_research_paper.tex.
